title: The RAD Float Trap: Why a Full Residential Aged Care Facility Can Still Run Short on Cash
excerpt: A fully occupied aged care facility can still hit a genuine cash squeeze. The reason rarely shows up in the trading figures. It sits inside the RAD pool, the deposits owed back to residents who leave.
content:
A residential aged care facility with every bed filled and a waitlist behind it looks, on paper, like a business with no cash problem. The AN-ACC funding is flowing, the daily fees are being collected, and the occupancy board could not look healthier. Ask the operator to name their actual cash position for next month, though, and the confidence usually drops. The reason sits in a part of the balance sheet that rarely gets discussed alongside occupancy and funding: the pool of refundable accommodation deposits sitting behind the front door.

A Refundable Accommodation Deposit, the RAD, is not revenue. It is a lump sum a resident or their family pays the facility in exchange for a room, structured as an amount the facility must eventually repay when the resident leaves. Some residents choose a Daily Accommodation Payment instead, which behaves more like rent and is not refundable, and many choose a blend of both. Either way, a meaningful share of the money sitting in a facility's bank account belongs, eventually, to the resident who paid it, not to the business holding it.

That distinction rarely causes a problem while departures are spread evenly across the year. It becomes a genuine cash event the moment several long-stay residents, often the ones who arrived with the largest deposits years ago, leave within a short window of each other. The facility can be as full as it has ever been and still be short of cash, because occupancy and a healthy RAD float are two different things being read as one number.

Two Different Pools of Money Sitting in the Same Account

Operating income for a residential aged care facility comes from two places: the AN-ACC subsidy the government pays according to each resident's assessed care needs, and the accommodation and daily living fees residents pay directly. That income funds staffing, food, maintenance and the day-to-day running of the facility, and it behaves the way most operators expect it to, arriving in a predictable rhythm and getting spent in a predictable rhythm.

The RAD pool behaves nothing like that. It arrives in large, irregular lump sums whenever a new resident moves in, and it leaves in large, irregular lump sums whenever a resident moves out or passes away. Because both pools of money sit in the same bank account, and because the RAD pool is usually the larger of the two on the balance sheet, it is easy for the day-to-day trading position to look stronger than it actually is. A facility drawing on the RAD pool to fund operating shortfalls, even informally and without anyone deciding to do so, is spending money it does not actually own.

Why a Handful of Departures Can Move More Cash Than a Year of Trading

The obligation to refund a RAD is not optional and it does not wait for convenient timing. Once a resident leaves permanently, the facility is required to repay the deposit within a fixed period, regardless of whether a new resident has moved into the room and regardless of how the rest of the facility is trading that month. A single long-held RAD can represent a substantial cash outflow on its own. Several landing in the same quarter, which happens more often than operators expect given the age profile of long-stay residents, can outweigh a full quarter of operating surplus.

The pattern that catches operators out is that a new resident moving into the vacated room does not solve the timing problem. Their RAD, if they pay one at all, arrives on its own schedule, often weeks or months after the room is filled, and is frequently a different amount to the deposit that just left. The facility can be at full occupancy the entire time and still be managing a genuine liquidity gap in the weeks between one deposit leaving and the next one arriving.

Reading Occupancy and Cash as Two Separate Questions

The fix is not complicated, but it does require treating the RAD pool as its own forecasting problem rather than folding it into the general bank balance. A rolling cash flow view that separates operating trading from RAD movements, built out to a horizon long enough to see refund obligations coming, changes a facility's ability to plan for a cluster of departures rather than discovering one in the account balance. This is precisely the discipline behind a 13-Week Cash Flow Build, applied to a sector where the largest cash movements often have nothing to do with how well the facility traded that week.

For an operator carrying substantial RAD liabilities against ageing accommodation stock, the same clarity changes how the facility looks to a bank or, eventually, to a buyer. A lender assessing facility limits, or a purchaser weighing up what the business is actually worth, both want to see operating profitability and RAD liability reported as separate lines, not blended into one balance that looks healthier than either half really is on its own.

Residential aged care is one of the few sectors where a fully occupied facility can still be cash constrained, and the two figures owners are told to watch, occupancy and revenue, do not answer the cash question on their own. Knowing what the RAD pool owes, and when, is the difference between a facility that manages a run of departures calmly and one that is caught out by it. That is the kind of pattern a fractional CFO brings into the monthly numbers conversation for facilities carrying meaningful RAD balances.

faqs.q: What is a RAD in residential aged care and why does it matter?
faqs.a: A Refundable Accommodation Deposit, or RAD, is a lump sum a resident pays a residential aged care facility for their room, which the facility must eventually repay when the resident leaves. It sits on the balance sheet as a liability rather than revenue, and it moves in large, irregular amounts that have nothing to do with how the facility is trading week to week. Treating it as ordinary cash on hand is where most of the confusion starts.

faqs.q: Why can a fully occupied aged care facility still run short of cash?
faqs.a: Occupancy measures whether rooms are filled, not whether the facility can meet its RAD refund obligations. A resident's departure triggers a repayment due within a fixed period regardless of whether a new resident has moved in or how strong that month's trading has been. Several departures close together can create a genuine cash gap even while every bed is filled. Building the kind of cash flow discipline that separates the two answers the question before it becomes urgent.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a RAD and a Daily Accommodation Payment?
faqs.a: A RAD is a lump sum deposit that the facility must eventually refund. A Daily Accommodation Payment, or DAP, is a periodic payment that functions more like rent and is not refundable. Many residents choose a mix of the two, paying part of the accommodation cost as a smaller lump sum and the balance as an ongoing daily payment, which changes the size and timing of the eventual RAD refund obligation for that room.

faqs.q: How can a residential aged care provider forecast upcoming RAD refund obligations?
faqs.a: The starting point is a rolling cash flow forecast that treats RAD movements as a separate line from operating income and expenses, built out far enough to see known long-stay residents and typical refund timing coming. A 13-Week Cash Flow Build applied to a facility's specific resident profile turns a number that normally only shows up as a surprise in the bank balance into something that can be planned for months ahead.

faqs.q: Should a residential aged care facility keep RAD funds separate from operating cash?
faqs.a: Legally the funds sit in the same accounts, but treating them as functionally separate from operating cash is what protects the business commercially. The pattern we see across the sector is that facilities reporting on RAD liabilities and operating cash flow as two distinct lines make calmer, better timed decisions than those reading a single combined bank balance as their true cash position.

faqs.q: How does the AN-ACC funding model affect a residential aged care facility's income?
faqs.a: AN-ACC, the Australian National Aged Care Classification, sets the government subsidy a facility receives for each resident based on their assessed care needs, alongside the accommodation and daily living fees residents pay directly. That combined income funds staffing and day-to-day operations and behaves predictably compared with the RAD pool, which is exactly why the two are often mistaken for one steady stream of cash rather than two very different ones.

faqs.q: When should an aged care provider get outside help managing its cash position?
faqs.a: Once a facility is carrying meaningful RAD balances against multiple long-stay residents, it is worth building a cash flow view that separates operating trading from deposit movements well before a cluster of departures forces the question. A fractional CFO engagement brings that discipline into the monthly numbers conversation without requiring a full-time finance hire.
